lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Every 3D game, physics simulation and data tool leans on the same quiet ingredient: linear algebra. Antoine's Dimension project puts it at the center.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Linear algebra. That's the matrices-and-vectors stuff, right?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. The heart of the repository is mathlib, a Rust crate for dense and sparse linear algebra, matrix decompositions, 3D math, clustering, graph algorithms and transforms.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A dense matrix stores every number. A sparse one stores only the non-zero entries, like a seating chart that lists just the occupied seats. That saves a lot of space when most of the grid is empty.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And it runs in the browser too?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It does. There are WebAssembly demos, plus optional SIMD and GPU features for speed. The wider Dimension repository wraps the crate with kinematics, physics, rendering experiments and documentation.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The quickest way is right on the project page: it runs the render, geometry and math demos in your browser, compiled to WebAssembly. To build it yourself, two commands from the mathlib folder: cargo build, then cargo test. The README and the docs folder cover the architecture and examples, and mathlib is published on docs dot r s.
